h1: Cross-training bar staff to help in the brewery
title: Cross-Training Bar Staff for the Brewery | Craft Beer School
desc: How to cross-train brewpub bar staff to help in the brewery safely: the tasks that suit them, the ones that do not and how to train and pay for it.
teaser: Your bartenders spend their quiet afternoons polishing glasses. Some of them would rather wash kegs. The brewer would love the help.
standfirst: Most brewpubs have a busy bar at night and a short-staffed brewery by day. Cross-training a few bar staff to help in the brewhouse fills gaps, builds a better team and gives ambitious people somewhere to grow. It only works if the safety lines are clear.
sections:
A brewpub with one brewer and one assistant has no cover when either is sick, on leave or tied up with a problem batch. Bar staff are already on site, already know the beer and often have quiet hours before evening service. Training two or three of them to help with basic brewery tasks gives you cover without a new hire.

It also improves the bar. Staff who have washed kegs and filled them understand why a keg should be handled carefully and why lines must be cleaned on schedule. They sell the beer better because they have seen how it is made.

Start with low risk, routine jobs that free up the brewer's time:

  • Rinsing and inspecting kegs before they go into the keg washer.
  • Labelling and moving filled kegs into the cold room, with proper lifting technique or a trolley.
  • Carrying and stacking 25 kg malt bags in the store.
  • Logging cold room temperatures and checking CO2 cylinder levels.
  • Cleaning floors, drains and the outside of tanks.
  • Helping with packaging, such as growlers or cans, under supervision.

Each of these takes a few hours to learn and saves the brewer real time every week.
Tasks that stay with trained brewers

Some jobs should stay with the brewing team until a person has had full training and sign-off:

  • Anything on the hot side: mashing, the boil, transferring hot wort near 100 °C.
  • Cleaning in place with caustic at 70 to 80 °C or acid cleaners.
  • Opening, venting or entering any tank. Nobody enters a tank without a confined space procedure.
  • Changing pressures on fermenters or serving tanks.
  • Excise records and gauge readings.

Write these lines into the job description of anyone being cross-trained. Clear limits make people more confident, not less.

Use a simple training sheet for each task. List the steps, the safety points and the protective equipment needed. The brewer shows the task, the trainee does it with the brewer watching, then the trainee does it alone while the brewer checks. Once the brewer is happy, both sign the sheet.

Keep the sheets in the training file. They show who is trained for what, which matters when you build rosters. They also show inspectors that training is taken seriously. One floor detail worth teaching early: always purge a cleaned keg with CO2 before filling. Oxygen left in the keg stales the beer within weeks.

Before any brewery task, every cross-trained person needs basic safety training: where the eye wash station is, what caustic burns look like, how to lift safely, what to do if they smell gas or feel dizzy in the cold room and where the emergency stops are. Carbon dioxide is invisible, heavier than air and collects in low spaces, so a person feeling lightheaded in the cold room should leave first and report after.

Give each person their own goggles, gloves and safety boots. Shared kit tends to go missing just when it is needed.

Cross-training is extra work and extra responsibility. Pay for the training time and for the brewery hours. Some brewpubs add a small allowance for staff trained in brewery tasks. Others treat it as a step towards an assistant brewer role. Either works if it is clear and fair.

Do not use cross-training to quietly double someone's workload. If a bartender works a full night shift, they should not also be washing kegs at 10 am the next day.

After two or three months, look at whether cross-training has helped. Ask the brewer how many hours a week the trained staff save them. Check the cleaning and temperature logs for gaps. Ask the cross-trained staff what they enjoy and what worries them. A bartender who feels rushed in the cellar is a safety risk you want to hear about early.

Watch the bar as well. If evening service suffers because the best bartender is tired from a morning in the brewery, rebalance the roster. The aim is a team that covers its gaps, not one that moves the gap from the brewhouse to the bar.
Make it a path, not a favour

Some cross-trained bar staff will discover they love brewing. That is good news. A trainee who has spent six months helping in the cellar and asks good questions may be your next assistant brewer. Offer them more training, such as a brewing fundamentals course, with a clear route forward. Our guide to training bar staff to sell craft beer covers the front of house skills that pair with this.

Designing roles, training and rosters so the team covers itself is a core part of running a brewpub. It is easy to start and harder to sustain.

Your first step: ask your brewer to list five tasks a trained bartender could take off their hands this month.
faqs: Is it safe for bar staff to work in a brewery?
Yes, for low risk tasks with proper training and protective equipment. Hot side work, caustic cleaning and anything involving tanks should stay with trained brewers.
What brewery tasks can bar staff help with?
Keg rinsing and moving, malt bag handling, temperature logs, cleaning floors and helping with packaging under supervision.
Should cross-trained staff be paid extra?
Pay for training and brewery hours at least. Many brewpubs add an allowance or treat it as a step to an assistant brewer role.
